summary:
Centre-Val de Loire stands under France's national framework. Criminal law, the custody rules of the French Criminal Procedure Code, anti-discrimination law, identity-document rules and the law on marriage apply uniformly across French regions, and no source in the inventory records a departure specific to this region.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure is custodial. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, and placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents rather than lived gender. Trans women whose documents are marked male — the majority, who have not undergone sex-reassignment surgery — are therefore held in men's facilities. Each establishment then improvises its own arrangement: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, has stated that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee recalling inmates shouting "We don't want any women here!" alongside threats of violence, and describes the case of American trans woman Kara B. held in conditions Hazan called worrying.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It found that serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights persist in adult prisons, while none were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The national preventive mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.
localsOnly:
France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The Défenseur des droits' framework decision on trans rights sets out official guidance for service providers, drawing on case files and association testimony alongside the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey finding that 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory records no Centre-Val de Loire-specific enforcement data, no regional detention figures, and no regional border-crossing accounts for this region; the custodial and border findings cited here are national in scope and drawn from inspections and testimony located elsewhere in France. Whether the CGLPL's 2021 binding guidance has been implemented at any establishment in this region is unresolved and not sourced.

The current status of the Défenseur des droits' framework decision, including whether it has been updated since the 2023 EU survey it cites, is unresolved in the inventory. No source addresses hate-crime protection, bathroom access, or healthcare access for trans visitors in this region.
